Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: [Pointwise identity] Fix representatives of $a,b$. For every $x\in D$ the identity $\|a(x)+b(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}=\|a(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}+\|b(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle_{\mathbb C^{r}}$ holds by the expansion of the finite-dimensional inner product; by [F1] the three real functions $x\mapsto\|a(x)\|^{2}$, $\|b(x)\|^{2}$ and $\operatorname{Re}\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle$ are measurable, and the last is integrable because $|\operatorname{Re}\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle|\le\|a(x)\|\,\|b(x)\|$ with $\|a\|\,\|b\|\in L^{1}(dx)$; representatives differing on null sets change the identity only on a null set. This proves the pointwise assertion of (a).

[Incoherent law] Assume $\|a\|,\|b\|>0$. By [F2] each of $B\mapsto\int_{B}\|a\|^{2}dx$ and $B\mapsto\int_{B}\|b\|^{2}dx$ is a finite measure with positive total masses $\|a\|^{2}$ and $\|b\|^{2}$; by [F4] each normalized set function is a probability measure, and a convex combination with $w\in[0,1]$ of two probability measures is again a probability measure, because countable additivity is preserved and $w\cdot1+(1-w)\cdot1=1$. This is (c).

[Recorded weights] Applying [F3] with $h=W$ and $H=1$ gives $
u(D)=\int_{D}W\,d\mu\le\int_{D}1\,d\mu=1$ and $
u(B)\ge0$ for every $B$ because $W\ge0$; countable additivity of $
u$ follows from [F2] applied to the measure $\mu$. If $
u(D)>0$, [F4] makes $ ar
u$ a probability measure. For the finite family, $
u_{a}=\int_{D}W_{a}d\mu\ge0$ and $\sum_{a}
u_{a}=\int_{D}\sum_{a}W_{a}\,d\mu\le\int_{D}1\,d\mu=1$ by finite additivity and [F3]; if $\sum_{a}W_{a}=1$ pointwise, the middle integral equals $\mu(D)=1$. This is (d).

[Integrated identity] Let $B\in\mathcal A$. Integrating the identity of step 1.1 over $B$ is legitimate because all three terms are integrable on $B$ by step 1.1 and [F1]; the integral of the left side is $\int_{B}\|a+b\|^{2}dx$ and the integral of the right side is $\int_{B}\|a\|^{2}dx+\int_{B}\|b\|^{2}dx+2\operatorname{Re}\langle a,b\rangle_{B}$, which is the displayed identity of (a).

[Coherent law] Assume $\|a+b\|>0$. The set function $B\mapsto\int_{B}\|a+b\|^{2}dx$ is a finite measure with total mass $\|a+b\|^{2}$ by [F2], and $\|a+b\|^{2}\in(0,\infty)$; dividing by this constant gives a finite measure of total mass one, hence a probability measure by [F4], whose value at $B$ is $p_{\mathrm{coh}}(B)$ with denominator $N+2c$ by step 2.1 applied to $B=D$. This is (b).

[Coincidence criterion] Assume the hypotheses of (e), including $\|a+b\|>0$. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 with $w=w_{*}$, $p_{*}(B)=\frac{1}{N}\int_{B}(\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2})dx$ and $p_{\mathrm{coh}}(B)=\frac{\int_{B}(\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2})dx+2c(B)}{N+2c}$ with $c(B):=\operatorname{Re}\langle a,b\rangle_{B}$; since $N>0$ and $N+2c=\|a+b\|^{2}>0$, the equality $p_{\mathrm{coh}}(B)=p_{*}(B)$ is equivalent to $N c(B)=c\,M(B)$ for the finite measure $M(B):=\int_{B}(\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2})dx$. The signed measure $N c(\cdot)-c\,M(\cdot)$ vanishes on every $B\in\mathcal A$ if and only if its density $N\operatorname{Re}\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle_{\mathbb C^{r}}-c(\|a(x)\|^{2}+\|b(x)\|^{2})$ vanishes $dx$-almost everywhere by [F2], since a nonzero integrable density has a level set of strictly positive or strictly negative integral. This is the displayed criterion; if $\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle=0$ a.e., then $c=0$ and $c(B)=0$ for every $B$, so the laws coincide, and if $c=0$ the criterion reduces to $\operatorname{Re}\langle a(x),b(x)\rangle=0$ a.e. This proves (e), and steps 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 3.1 prove the remaining clauses.

citations.quote:
**(a) Framework data and state convention.** Adopt the state and composition
postulate P1, the observable and probability postulate P2, the kinematics and
one-particle model postulate P5, the identical-particle and spin postulate P6,
and the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]). Fix a spin label
$s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $r:=2s+1$, and fix a mass parameter
$m>0$. P5 assigns the one-particle state space
$$H_s:=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^r)$$
with almost-everywhere equivalence classes and pairing
$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{l=1}^r f_l(x)\overline{g_l(x)}\,dx,$$
linear in the first argument ([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). P1 identifies a pure
preparation with the ray $[\psi]:=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a
unit vector $\psi$ and a general preparation with a density operator, meaning a
bounded self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Write
$$D(H_s):=\{\rho:\rho\text{ is a bounded self-adjoint positive trace-class operator on }H_s\text{ and }\operatorname{tr}\rho=1\}$$
for the set of general preparations.

For a unit vector $u$, define $P_uf:=\langle f,u\rangle u$. By Cauchy--Schwarz
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]),
$\|P_uf\|=|\langle f,u\rangle|\le\|f\|$, so $P_u$ is bounded. Then
$P_u^2=P_u$ and $P_u$ is self-adjoint because for $f,g\in H_s$,
$\langle P_uf,g\rangle=\langle f,u\rangle\langle u,g\rangle
=\langle f,P_ug\rangle$. Moreover
$\langle P_uf,f\rangle=|\langle f,u\rangle|^2\ge0$ by the inner-product
identities and $\langle u,u\rangle=1$. Its range is $\mathbb C u$, so it has
finite rank and is trace class by [[def-trace-class-operator]]. The one-term
nuclear representation $P_uf=\langle f,u\rangle u$ gives
$\operatorname{tr}P_u=\langle u,u\rangle=1$ by
[[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]. Thus $P_u$ is a
density operator. For $\psi\ne0$ define
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=P_{\psi/\|\psi\|},\qquad \widehat\rho(\psi)f=\frac{\langle f,\psi\rangle\psi}{\|\psi\|^2}.$$
For every nonzero scalar $z$, conjugate-linearity in the second argument and
$\|z\psi\|^2=|z|^2\|\psi\|^2$ give
$$\widehat\rho(z\psi)f=\frac{\langle f,z\psi\rangle z\psi}{\|z\psi\|^2}=\frac{|z|^2\langle f,\psi\rangle\psi}{|z|^2\|\psi\|^2}=\widehat\rho(\psi)f,$$
so the pure density operator depends only on the ray.

**Position PVM and Born-density calculation.** P5 assigns the componentwise
position operators $Q_jf=x_jf$ on
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in H_s:x_jf\in H_s\},\qquad j=1,2,3.$$
Each $Q_j$ is self-adjoint on this domain. To see density, for $f\in H_s$ put
$f_n=\mathbf 1_{\{|x_j|\le n\}}f$; then $f_n\in D(Q_j)$ and $f_n\to f$ in
$H_s$ by dominated convergence. If $f,g\in D(Q_j)$, then
$\langle Q_jf,g\rangle=\langle f,Q_jg\rangle$ because $x_j$ is real-valued
and both products are integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz. If $g\in D(Q_j^*)$ with
$Q_j^*g=h$, let $E_n=\{x:|x_j|\le n\}$. For every $q\in H_s$ supported in
$E_n$, one has $q\in D(Q_j)$ and
$\langle q,(x_jg-h)\mathbf 1_{E_n}\rangle=0$ by the defining adjoint
identity. The vector $(x_jg-h)\mathbf 1_{E_n}$ lies in $H_s$ because $x_j$
is bounded on $E_n$; taking it for $q$ shows $x_jg=h$ almost everywhere on
$E_n$. Since $E_n\uparrow\mathbb R^3$, $x_jg=h\in H_s$ almost everywhere,
so $g\in D(Q_j)$ and $Q_j^*g=Q_jg$. Symmetry gives the reverse domain
inclusion; hence $Q_j=Q_j^*$ by
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]].

For a Borel set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, define the indicator multiplication
operator $M_{\mathbf 1_S}:H_s\to H_s$ by
$(M_{\mathbf 1_S}f)(x):=\mathbf 1_S(x)f(x)$ almost everywhere. This is
independent of the representative of the $L^2$ class and is bounded, since
$$\|M_{\mathbf 1_S}f\|^2=\int_S\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^r}^2dx\le\|f\|^2.$$
It is linear and a bounded operator with bound one
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). It is an orthogonal projection:
$\mathbf 1_S^2=\mathbf 1_S$ and the real indicator multiplier is
self-adjoint for the declared pairing.

For Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, define
$$E_j(C):=M_{\mathbf 1_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}}.$$
Each value is a bounded orthogonal projection since
$\|\mathbf 1_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}f\|\le\|f\|$, and
$E_j(\varnothing)=0$,
$E_j(\mathbb R)=I$, and $E_j(C\cap D)=E_j(C)E_j(D)$. For a disjoint sequence
$(C_n)$ with union $C$, the squared norm of
$E_j(C)f-\sum_{n\le N}E_j(C_n)f$ equals
$$\int_{\{x:x_j\in C\setminus\cup_{n\le N}C_n\}}\|f(x)\|^2dx,$$
which tends to zero by dominated convergence; hence $E_j$ is strongly
countably additive. Its scalar measures are finite Borel measures
$$\langle E_j(C)f,f\rangle=\int_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}\|f(x)\|^2dx,$$
and are regular on $\mathbb R$ by
[[cor-second-countable-lch-locally-finite-borel-measures-are-regular]]. The
push-forward integral identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R}g(\lambda)d\langle E_j(\lambda)f,f\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(x_j)\|f(x)\|^2dx$$
holds first for indicators and nonnegative simple functions and then for
nonnegative measurable $g$ by monotone convergence. In particular the domain
of $\int\lambda\,dE_j(\lambda)$ is exactly $D(Q_j)$ by the same identity
with $g(\lambda)=\lambda^2$. For bounded Borel $g$, the bounded PVM calculus
equals multiplication by $g(x_j)$: this holds for indicators by the
definition of $E_j$, for finite simple functions by linearity, and for bounded
Borel functions by uniform simple approximation and the norm bound of the
bounded calculus ([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]). Therefore the
truncations of the unbounded integral are multiplication by
$x_j\mathbf 1_{\{|x_j|\le n\}}$. For $f\in D(Q_j)$ these converge in $H_s$
to $x_jf$, since the squared tail norm is
$\int_{\{|x_j|>n\}}x_j^2\|f(x)\|^2dx\to0$ by dominated convergence. Thus
$\int\lambda\,dE_j(\lambda)=Q_j$ on exactly $D(Q_j)$, and the regular spectral
theorem identifies $E_j$ as the spectral PVM of $Q_j$
([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

Define the joint position PVM by
$$G(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_B}\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R^3\text{ Borel}).$$
For each $f$, $\|G(B)f\|\le\|f\|$, so its values are bounded; indicator
multiplication gives its projection, identity, and intersection laws. Strong
countable additivity follows from dominated convergence applied to $\|f\|^2$.
Its scalar measures are $B\mapsto\int_B\|f(x)\|^2dx$, finite
regular Borel measures on $\mathbb R^3$. On coordinate rectangles,
$$G(C_1\times C_2\times C_3)=E_1(C_1)E_2(C_2)E_3(C_3).$$
The rectangles generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$; the published Borel-product
and finite-measure uniqueness theorems show that these rectangle values
uniquely determine the joint PVM ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]],
[[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]],
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]): for any two candidate PVMs,
their finite scalar measures agree on the generating rectangles and on the
whole space, so they agree on every Borel set; the polarization identity in
the last lemma then gives equality of the operator values. This constructs the
mathematical joint position PVM; a physical joint detector reading is supplied
only for the finite effect families declared below. For a density operator
$\rho$ define
$\mu^G_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho G(B))$ for each Borel
$B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Since $G$ is a PVM, this set function is a probability
measure by the general density/PVM calculation used in clause (ii) of P2. For a
finite Borel partition $(B_a)_{a=1}^m$,
the operators $G(B_a)$ are orthogonal projections and sum to $I$. For each
$f\in H_s$,
$\langle G(B_a)f,f\rangle=\|G(B_a)f\|^2\in[0,\|f\|^2]$, so they are
bounded effects with $0\le G(B_a)\le I$ in quadratic-form order. Clause (iv)
of P2 therefore assigns the channel probabilities
$p_a(\rho)=\mu^G_\rho(B_a)$; the two-channel partition
$(B,\mathbb R^3\setminus B)$ assigns $\mu^G_\rho(B)$ to bin $B$
([[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]). Thus $G$ is the
mathematical joint position PVM, while the detector reading used here is the
declared finite-effect model of P2(iv); this does not assert that every three
sharp coordinate measurement is jointly realized by a laboratory apparatus.
For a unit vector $u$, the trace formula for the rank-one operator $P_u$ gives
$$\mu^G_{P_u}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(P_uG(B))=\|G(B)u\|^2=\int_B\|u(x)\|_{\mathbb C^r}^2dx,$$
and P7(iii) leaves identification of this ideal detector with a concrete
apparatus as a tested physical claim with uncertainty.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as required by
the cited trace and spectral suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it.

**(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), meaning $D(A)=D(A^*)$ and $A\psi=A^*\psi$ on this common domain, together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable.

**(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$
By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). **(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. **(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of effects on $H$ as defined above, with $\sum_aF_a=I$. The **outcome probabilities** are $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$. They are normalized for every state space assigned by P1, as shown by the preceding general-$H$ calculation. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3).

**(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

$$H_s:=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^r)$$
with almost-everywhere equivalence classes and pairing
$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{l=1}^r f_l(x)\overline{g_l(x)}\,dx,$$

[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). P1 identifies a pure

bounded self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Write

For a unit vector $u$, define $P_uf:=\langle f,u\rangle u$. By Cauchy--Schwarz
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]),
$\|P_uf\|=|\langle f,u\rangle|\le\|f\|$, so $P_u$ is bounded. Then
$P_u^2=P_u$ and $P_u$ is self-adjoint because for $f,g\in H_s$,
$\langle P_uf,g\rangle=\langle f,u\rangle\langle u,g\rangle
=\langle f,P_ug\rangle$. Moreover
$\langle P_uf,f\rangle=|\langle f,u\rangle|^2\ge0$ by the inner-product
identities and $\langle u,u\rangle=1$. Its range is $\mathbb C u$, so it has
finite rank and is trace class by [[def-trace-class-operator]]. The one-term
nuclear representation $P_uf=\langle f,u\rangle u$ gives
$\operatorname{tr}P_u=\langle u,u\rangle=1$ by
[[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]. Thus $P_u$ is a
density operator. For $\psi\ne0$ define
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=P_{\psi/\|\psi\|},\qquad \widehat\rho(\psi)f=\frac{\langle f,\psi\rangle\psi}{\|\psi\|^2}.$$
For every nonzero scalar $z$, conjugate-linearity in the second argument and
$\|z\psi\|^2=|z|^2\|\psi\|^2$ give
$$\widehat\rho(z\psi)f=\frac{\langle f,z\psi\rangle z\psi}{\|z\psi\|^2}=\frac{|z|^2\langle f,\psi\rangle\psi}{|z|^2\|\psi\|^2}=\widehat\rho(\psi)f,$$
so the pure density operator depends only on the ray.

position operators $Q_jf=x_jf$ on
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in H_s:x_jf\in H_s\},\qquad j=1,2,3.$$
Each $Q_j$ is self-adjoint on this domain. To see density, for $f\in H_s$ put
$f_n=\mathbf 1_{\{|x_j|\le n\}}f$; then $f_n\in D(Q_j)$ and $f_n\to f$ in
$H_s$ by dominated convergence. If $f,g\in D(Q_j)$, then
$\langle Q_jf,g\rangle=\langle f,Q_jg\rangle$ because $x_j$ is real-valued
and both products are integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz. If $g\in D(Q_j^*)$ with
$Q_j^*g=h$, let $E_n=\{x:|x_j|\le n\}$. For every $q\in H_s$ supported in
$E_n$, one has $q\in D(Q_j)$ and
$\langle q,(x_jg-h)\mathbf 1_{E_n}\rangle=0$ by the defining adjoint
identity. The vector $(x_jg-h)\mathbf 1_{E_n}$ lies in $H_s$ because $x_j$
is bounded on $E_n$; taking it for $q$ shows $x_jg=h$ almost everywhere on
$E_n$. Since $E_n\uparrow\mathbb R^3$, $x_jg=h\in H_s$ almost everywhere,
so $g\in D(Q_j)$ and $Q_j^*g=Q_jg$. Symmetry gives the reverse domain
inclusion; hence $Q_j=Q_j^*$ by
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]].

For a Borel set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, define the indicator multiplication
operator $M_{\mathbf 1_S}:H_s\to H_s$ by
$(M_{\mathbf 1_S}f)(x):=\mathbf 1_S(x)f(x)$ almost everywhere. This is
independent of the representative of the $L^2$ class and is bounded, since
$$\|M_{\mathbf 1_S}f\|^2=\int_S\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^r}^2dx\le\|f\|^2.$$
It is linear and a bounded operator with bound one
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). It is an orthogonal projection:
$\mathbf 1_S^2=\mathbf 1_S$ and the real indicator multiplier is
self-adjoint for the declared pairing.

For Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, define
$$E_j(C):=M_{\mathbf 1_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}}.$$
Each value is a bounded orthogonal projection since
$\|\mathbf 1_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}f\|\le\|f\|$, and
$E_j(\varnothing)=0$,
$E_j(\mathbb R)=I$, and $E_j(C\cap D)=E_j(C)E_j(D)$. For a disjoint sequence
$(C_n)$ with union $C$, the squared norm of
$E_j(C)f-\sum_{n\le N}E_j(C_n)f$ equals
$$\int_{\{x:x_j\in C\setminus\cup_{n\le N}C_n\}}\|f(x)\|^2dx,$$
which tends to zero by dominated convergence; hence $E_j$ is strongly
countably additive. Its scalar measures are finite Borel measures
$$\langle E_j(C)f,f\rangle=\int_{\{x:x_j\in C\}}\|f(x)\|^2dx,$$
and are regular on $\mathbb R$ by
[[cor-second-countable-lch-locally-finite-borel-measures-are-regular]]. The
push-forward integral identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R}g(\lambda)d\langle E_j(\lambda)f,f\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(x_j)\|f(x)\|^2dx$$
holds first for indicators and nonnegative simple functions and then for
nonnegative measurable $g$ by monotone convergence. In particular the domain
of $\int\lambda\,dE_j(\lambda)$ is exactly $D(Q_j)$ by the same identity
with $g(\lambda)=\lambda^2$. For bounded Borel $g$, the bounded PVM calculus
equals multiplication by $g(x_j)$: this holds for indicators by the
definition of $E_j$, for finite simple functions by linearity, and for bounded
Borel functions by uniform simple approximation and the norm bound of the
bounded calculus ([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]). Therefore the
truncations of the unbounded integral are multiplication by
$x_j\mathbf 1_{\{|x_j|\le n\}}$. For $f\in D(Q_j)$ these converge in $H_s$
to $x_jf$, since the squared tail norm is
$\int_{\{|x_j|>n\}}x_j^2\|f(x)\|^2dx\to0$ by dominated convergence. Thus
$\int\lambda\,dE_j(\lambda)=Q_j$ on exactly $D(Q_j)$, and the regular spectral
theorem identifies $E_j$ as the spectral PVM of $Q_j$
([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or

derivations.claim: [Coherent law] Assume admissibility at $\varphi$ and put $u=(\psi_1+e^{i\varphi}\psi_2)/\|\psi_1+e^{i\varphi}\psi_2\|$. Then $\rho_{\mathrm{coh}}(\varphi)=\widehat\rho(u)$ by [F3], and [F1] gives $$\mu^G_{\rho_{\mathrm{coh}}(\varphi)}(B)=\int_B\|u(x)\|^2dx=\frac{\int_B\|\psi_1(x)+e^{i\varphi}\psi_2(x)\|^2dx}{\|\psi_1+e^{i\varphi}\psi_2\|^2}.$$ Applying [F4] with $a=\psi_1$ and $b=e^{i\varphi}\psi_2$ expands the numerator; conjugate-linearity in the second argument gives the factor $e^{-i\varphi}$. At $B=\mathbb R^3$ the denominator is $N+2\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\varphi}Z)>0$. This proves (a).

[Which-path law] Let $\rho_j=\widehat\rho(\psi_j)$ and $u_j=\psi_j/\|\psi_j\|$. By [F1], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_jG(B))=\int_B\|u_j(x)\|^2dx=\|\psi_j\|^{-2}\int_B\|\psi_j(x)\|^2dx$. The declared mixture is $w\rho_1+(1-w)\rho_2$ by [F3]; applying trace linearity [F2] to P2's outcome formula yields (b).

[Coincidence criterion] Assume admissibility at phase $0$, and define $M(B)=\int_B(\|\psi_1(x)\|^2+\|\psi_2(x)\|^2)dx$ and $c_B=\operatorname{Re}\int_B\langle\psi_1(x),\psi_2(x)\rangle dx$. By [F4], the zero-phase coherent law is $(M(B)+2c_B)/(N+2c)$, while step 1.2 at $w=w_*$ gives the which-path law $M(B)/N$. Since $N>0$ and $N+2c=\|\psi_1+\psi_2\|^2>0$, equality of these laws for every Borel $B$ is equivalent to $N c_B=cM(B)$ for every $B$. Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it.

**(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), meaning $D(A)=D(A^*)$ and $A\psi=A^*\psi$ on this common domain, together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable.

**(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$
By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). It is the general form of the Born rule adopted here.

**(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. An ideal point value is an idealization; a real detector reports a finite-resolution outcome, that is, the probability of a declared Borel set $B$ such as a bin, and the recorded-event probability is that of (ii) for the bin, not the value of a density at a point.

**(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of effects on $H$ as defined above, with $\sum_aF_a=I$. The **outcome probabilities** are $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$. They are normalized for every state space assigned by P1, as shown by the preceding general-$H$ calculation. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3).

**(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

Adopt the declared two-path preparation model of
[[def-nrqm-interference-two-path-preparation-and-detection-model]], the
unsharp finite-outcome clause (iv) of the observable and probability postulate
P2, and the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]). Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The following vocabulary is used
by this page.

**(a) Declared recorded detector.** A **declared recorded detector** of the
arrangement is a finite set $A$ of **recorded outcome labels** with
$0\notin A$, together with measurable **recorded weights**
$w_{a}:\mathbb R^{3}\to[0,1]$ for $a\in A$ such that
$\sum_{a\in A}w_{a}(x)\le1$ for almost every $x\in\mathbb R^{3}$. The
**effect** of the label $a$ is the multiplication operator
$$F_{a}:=M_{w_{a}},\qquad (M_{w}\psi)(x):=w(x)\psi(x)\quad\text{a.e.},$$
on $H_{s}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$, and the **no-record effect** is
$$F_{0}:=I-\sum_{a\in A}F_{a}.$$
The multiplier is a well-defined linear map on almost-everywhere classes,
since changing a representative on a null set changes its product only on
that null set.
Each $F_a$ is bounded: for $\psi\in H_s$,
$$\|M_{w_a}\psi\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_a(x)^2\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^r}^2dx\le\|\psi\|^2,$$
so the boundedness inequality holds with bound $C=1$ by monotonicity of the
nonnegative integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).
Thus $F_a$ is a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Because $w_a$
is real, the componentwise pairing gives
$\langle M_{w_a}\psi,\phi\rangle=\langle\psi,M_{w_a}\phi\rangle$ for all
$\psi,\phi\in H_s$; hence $F_a$ is self-adjoint by
[[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]. At almost every $x$, the finite-dimensional
operator $w_a(x)I_{\mathbb C^r}$ is nonnegative in the sense of
[[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]], and therefore
$$0\le\langle F_a\psi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_a(x)\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^r}^2dx\le\|\psi\|^2.$$
Here $0\le F_a\le I$ means these quadratic-form inequalities for every
$\psi\in H_s$.

Define $w_0(x):=\max\{0,1-\sum_{a\in A}w_a(x)\}$. This is measurable,
$0\le w_0\le1$, and it equals $1-\sum_aw_a$ almost everywhere by the
admissibility condition. Thus $F_0=M_{w_0}=I-\sum_aF_a$ on $H_s$, and the
same argument gives $0\le F_0\le I$ and self-adjointness. Consequently
$\sum_{a\in A}F_a+F_0=I$, so the completed family is a finite family of
bounded effects of clause (iv) of P2
([[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]).

**(b) Recorded probabilities.** For a preparation $\rho\in D(H_{s})$ the
**recorded probability** of a label $a\in A$ and the **no-record probability**
are
$$\nu(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho F_{a}\bigr),\qquad \nu(0):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho F_{0}\bigr)=1-\sum_{a\in A}\nu(a),$$
the outcome reading of clause (iv) of P2 for the declared effects
([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (f)
records the reading; the numbers are nonnegative and sum to one). The
**recorded-event mass** is $\nu(A):=\sum_{a\in A}\nu(a)=1-\nu(0)\in[0,1]$. A
detector is **full-efficiency** when $\sum_{a}w_{a}=1$ almost everywhere, so
that $F_{0}=0$ and $\nu(0)=0$ for every preparation. For a fixed preparation
$\rho$, the model **loses** events when $\nu(0)>0$, and the no-record channel
carries this lost mass. A detector that is not full-efficiency can nevertheless
have $\nu(0)=0$ for a particular preparation. A **declared recorded bin** $B$ is
the special case with one label $a$ and $w_{a}=\mathbf 1_{B}$; then
$F_{a}=G(B)$ is the position projection of clause (e) of
[[def-nrqm-interference-two-path-preparation-and-detection-model]], with the
position set $B$ read in the metre unit of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], and the recorded probability is
the ideal bin probability.

**(c) Loss conditioning.** When $\nu(A)>0$, the **conditioned recorded law** is
$$\bar\nu(a):=\frac{\nu(a)}{\nu(A)}\qquad(a\in A).$$
It is a probability measure on the finite set $A$
([[def-probability-measure]]); it is the law of the recorded label under the
declared model conditioned on the occurrence of a record. Conditioning is a
statistical operation on the recorded data; it is not a state update, and no
claim of P3 is made here.

**(d) Sampling model.** A **declared $N$-trial sampling model** for a fixed
preparation $\rho$ is a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$
carrying measurable maps
$O_{1},\dots,O_{N}:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to
(A\cup\{0\},\mathcal P(A\cup\{0\}))$ ($N\ge1$), where $0$ is the no-record
label of clause (b) and is distinct from every recorded label because
$0\notin A$. The maps are **mutually independent** in the sense of
[[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]] and **identically distributed**
with $\mathbb P(O_{k}=a)=\nu(a)$ for every $a\in A$, $\mathbb P(O_{k}=0)=\nu(0)$
and every $k$, where $\nu$ is the recorded law of clause (b); the numbers
$\nu(a)$ and $\nu(0)$ sum to one, so this is a probability law on the finite
set $A\cup\{0\}$. The **empirical frequency** of the label $a$ in the sample is
$$F_{N}(a):=\frac{1}{N}\#\{k:O_{k}=a\}.$$
A **declared fringe criterion** for sample size $N$ is a subset
$C\subseteq(A\cup\{0\})^{N}$; the model **accepts** the sample when
$(O_{1},\dots,O_{N})\in C$ and **fails the criterion** otherwise. The
identification of repetitions of a concrete procedure with the independent
identically distributed model is an additional statistical assumption in the
sense of clause (ii) of P7; it is not a consequence of P1-P6, and correlated
trials, drifting preparation, dead time and selection must be modeled or
recorded as limitations if present ([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]).

**(e) Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) fix the recorded-detector and sampling
vocabulary of the pair and read clause (iv) of P2 and clauses (i)-(iii) of P7.
The recorded weights, the label set, the conditioning convention and the
sampling model are declared apparatus and procedure inputs. The claim "this
apparatus realizes the effect family $F_{a}$" and the claim "its repetitions
are independent and identically distributed draws of $\nu$" are physical
identifications with uncertainty under P7(iii) and P7(ii), can fail, and are
not derived here. No calibration, efficiency, background or resolution value
is asserted, no counts are recorded, and no statistical-inference conclusion
is drawn by this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

   and

   ([[def-operator-norm]]);

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the observable and probability
postulate P2, the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5 and the
internal-factor postulate P6, as read by
[[def-nrqm-interference-two-path-preparation-and-detection-model]], and the
preparation and apparatus discipline P7, and adopt the declared two-path

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following kinematics and one-particle model. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited operator suppliers.

**(i) Spacetime and frames.** The model reads its events and frames in the Newtonian arena of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]], with inertial frames and frame changes as in [[def-nrqm-framework-inertial-frames]]: the frame changes are the Galilean transformations of [[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]], and their composition is governed by the group law of [[lem-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations-form-a-group]]. These frames are global coordinate charts, not observer congruences and not time-varying basis fields. The parameters of a frame change are read in the units fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]].

**(ii) Apparatus motion.** The macroscopic constituents of preparations and apparatus are described by the classical trajectories of [[def-nrqm-framework-classical-apparatus-trajectories]]; a quantum particle of the model is not assigned a worldline between preparations and detections.

**(iii) One-particle state space.** For one particle of spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and mass parameter $m>0$, the model uses the state space
$$H_{s}:=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\widehat\otimes\,\mathbb C^{2s+1}\cong L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{2s+1}\bigr),$$
whose second factor carries the spin representation assigned in the postulate P6, and $\hbar>0$ is the action constant of the adopted unit system. Position and momentum act on $H_s$ componentwise: for $\psi=(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_{2s+1})$ the $j$-th position acts by $(Q_j\psi)_l(x):=x_j\psi_l(x)$ on the classes with $x_j\psi_l\in L^2$, and the $k$-th momentum by $(P_k\psi)_l:=-i\hbar D_k\psi_l$ on the classes whose componentwise weak derivative lies in $L^2$; for one component these are the operators of [[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], whose self-adjointness, domains and Fourier representation are supplied by [[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]]. On the componentwise Schwartz space defined in the preceding mathematical realization, the canonical commutation relation $(Q_jP_k-P_kQ_j)\psi=i\hbar\delta_{jk}\psi$ holds componentwise by [[lem-nrqm-framework-ccr-on-the-schwartz-core]] ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

**(iv) Baseline Hamiltonian.** For a real bounded measurable potential $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ the model uses the scalar Hamiltonian
$$H_{\mathrm{op}}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta+V(Q),\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{op}})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\ \text{(componentwise)},$$
with the free part $-\hbar^{2}\Delta/2m$ and the bounded multiplier $V(Q)$ as in [[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]] clauses (b) and (c) ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]); that theorem supplies the self-adjointness of each component operator on the displayed domain and the strongly continuous unitary group it generates, which the dynamics postulate P4 then reads as the evolution. The assignment of the operator $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ to a particle of mass $m$ and spin $s$ is the physical content of this clause; the mathematical properties are those of the cited theorem.

**(v) What is separate.** The model does not follow from P1-P4: the choice of the Newtonian arena, of the frame class, of the tensor factor $\mathbb C^{2s+1}$, of the operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ as position and momentum and of the Hamiltonian of clause (iv) are all adopted. Singular or unbounded model potentials (Coulomb-type, oscillator-type, boundary and point-interaction realizations) are separate model choices with their own domains and self-adjointness statements, established before use; relativistic matter, massless particles and radiation modes are not supplied by this massive-model assignment; they are adopted separately on their own pages, without a limiting construction here. No empirical identification of a particular particle species with a value of $s$ or $m$ is made or recorded here; the species parameters are empirical inputs in the sense of P6 and P7.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the framework. They assert that the model is used in the nonrelativistic regime and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by it; no numerical measurement is recorded.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statement of isolated autonomous dynamics. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and group suppliers.

**(i) Energy operator.** An **isolated autonomous system** of the sector has a declared **energy operator** $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ that is self-adjoint ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and a declared energy unit in which its spectral coordinate is read. The energy operator is part of the model specification of the system; for a massive particle it is fixed by the kinematics postulate P5, and singular or unbounded model Hamiltonians require their own self-adjointness statements.

**(ii) Evolution.** The time evolution of the model is the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad U(t+s)=U(t)U(s),\quad U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1},$$
defined by the spectral calculus of the self-adjoint generator ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The energy unit enters the argument of the exponential so that $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ acts in the dimensionless spectral variable.

**(iii) State evolution.** A vector state evolves continuously, $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the Schroedinger equation
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(t)$$
holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, where the derivative is the norm limit of the difference quotients; for other vectors the equation is not asserted, although the evolution remains continuous. A density-operator preparation evolves as $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$, which is a density operator for every $t$ and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho(t)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

**(iv) Time-dependent families.** A prescribed time-dependent family $t\mapsto H(t)$ of self-adjoint operators is a different model assumption: a norm-continuous finite-dimensional Hermitian family is used only through the unitary two-time propagator that its family defines, and the exponential of the integral of $H(t)$ is not identified with that propagator unless the family commutes with itself at different times. The general unbounded time-dependent case requires a separate existence and domain theorem of its own and is not adopted by this postulate; the driven-dynamics page states its own assumptions for the models it treats.

**(v) Open systems.** A non-unitary evolution of the reduced description of a system coupled to an environment is an extension obtained from an explicitly chosen environment model and a declared reduction, not a replacement for clause (ii); no environment model is adopted by this postulate.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the isolated-system idealization. They assert nothing about the origin of the energy operator of a concrete system, about the accuracy of the idealization for a laboratory preparation, or about which laboratory interactions realize an isolated evolution; those are tested identifications in the sense of P7.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).
